title: Designing with Modern Transistors
intro: In a 40 nm process the square law can be off by a large factor, so devices are sized from simulated curves of a reference transistor and then scaled. This page covers the short-channel effects behind that, how $g_m$ can be raised, and a systematic sizing procedure (Razavi, Sections 11.1 to 11.4).

blocks.text: Why the square law fails

For a 5 µm/40 nm NMOS, a best-fit square-law model and the real BSIM characteristics diverge visibly, the curves have no clean saturation region, and for overdrives from 50 to 350 mV the knee sits below $V_{DS} = 0.2$ V. Two mobility effects are mainly responsible.
Velocity saturation

Carrier velocity stops rising with the lateral field above about 1 V/µm (velocities near $10^7$ cm/s); a 40 nm channel at 1 V is well beyond that. In the extreme case where carriers travel at $v_{sat}$ from the source onward, $I = Q_d v$ with $Q_d = WC_{ox}(V_{GS} - V_{TH})$ gives
The current is linear in overdrive and independent of $L$, saturation arrives at a $V_{DS}$ below the overdrive, and $g_m$ is roughly constant with bias.
Mobility degradation
A stronger vertical field also lowers mobility. Model it as $\mu = \mu_0/[1 + \theta(V_{GS} - V_{TH})]$; then
For $\theta(V_{GS} - V_{TH}) \ll 1$ this is the square-law $g_m$; for large overdrive it flattens to $\frac{1}{2}\mu_0C_{ox}(W/L)/\theta$.

blocks.alt: Plot of normalized transconductance against overdrive from 0 to 0.6 V. The square-law line rises straight to 0.6. Curves for theta of 1, 2 and 4 per volt bend over and level off at about 0.3, 0.2 and 0.11.
blocks.caption: Larger $\theta$, flatter $g_m$: raising the overdrive stops buying transconductance.

blocks.text: Ways to raise $g_m$

From $g_m = \mu C_{ox}(W/L)(V_{GS} - V_{TH}) = \sqrt{2\mu C_{ox}(W/L)I_D} = 2I_D/(V_{GS} - V_{TH})$, fix one of $W/L$, overdrive or $I_D$ and vary the other two. Raising $W/L$ and $I_D$ together at constant overdrive scales $g_m$ and $I_D$ linearly for any device law, because a $K$ times wider device carrying $K$ times the current is just $K$ copies in parallel; the current density $I_D/W$, the overdrive and $g_m/I_D$ stay put. Raising $W/L$ at constant current lowers the overdrive and helps until the device reaches subthreshold, where $g_m \to I_D/(\xi V_T)$ no matter the width. Raising $I_D$ at fixed $W/L$ raises the overdrive and eats headroom.

With a 1 V supply the overdrive is capped at a few hundred millivolts, so the usual sequence is: widen while it helps, add current when width stops helping, and widen again when the overdrive limit is hit, i.e. scale width and current together.
The reference-transistor method

Simulate one reference device, e.g. $W_{REF}/L_{min} = 5\,\mu$m/40 nm, once: $I_D$-$V_{DS}$ curves for overdrives from about 50 to 600 mV in 50 mV steps, $g_m$ against overdrive and against $I_D$, and $r_O$ against $I_D$. Every transistor of that length is then a scaled copy. Design problems specify two of $I_D$, $V_{DS,min}$ (taken equal to the overdrive) and $g_m$:

items: Given $I_D$ and $V_{DS,min}$: read the reference current at $V_{GS} - V_{TH} = V_{DS} = V_{DS,min}$, scale the width by $I_D/I_{D,REF}$, and scale $g_m$ (and divide $r_O$) by the same factor. If $g_m$ is too small, raise $I_D$ and $W$. Choosing the overdrive equal to $V_{DS,min}$ (not higher) maximises $g_m$ for a given current, since $g_m = 2I_D/(V_{GS} - V_{TH})$, even though the device gets wider.

Given $g_m$ and $I_D$: first check that $g_m < I_D/(\xi V_T)$, otherwise it is impossible at that current. On the $g_m$-$I_D$ plot draw a line from the origin through the target; it crosses the reference curve at the reference bias point (its slope is $g_m/I_D$, so the overdrive is fixed along it). Scale $W$ by the ratio of the two points. If the resulting overdrive is too large for the headroom, pick a lower overdrive point on the curve and scale to the full current; $g_m$ then comes out above the target.
Given $g_m$ and $V_{DS,min}$: read $g_{m,REF}$ and $I_{D,REF}$ at that overdrive and scale both by $g_m/g_{m,REF}$. If the current is too high, fall back to the previous case.
Given only $g_m$: pick a reasonable overdrive (say 200 mV), read the reference point, scale; if the current is excessive, try 150 mV.

blocks.alt: Plot of gm against ID up to 1.2 mA. A blue curve for the reference width rises steeply then flattens to about 5 mS. A dashed red line from the origin marks the weak-inversion limit. A black line from the origin passes through the reference curve at about 195 microamps and 1.9 millisiemens and continues to a target point at 1 mA and 10 mS.
blocks.caption: Scaling along a constant-$g_m/I_D$ line. Points above the weak-inversion line cannot be reached at any width.

blocks.text: This is the $g_m/I_D$ method in a graphical form. In strong inversion $g_m/I_D = 2/(V_{GS} - V_{TH})$; it saturates near $1/(\xi V_T)$, about 25 V⁻¹, in weak inversion. High $g_m/I_D$ (15 to 25 V⁻¹) gives the most transconductance per microamp, for low-noise and high-gain devices, but is slow and large; low $g_m/I_D$ (5 to 10 V⁻¹) is fast but costs current.
Choosing the channel length

If the $r_O$ obtained is too low, lengthen the device and widen it in proportion. The scaling is not exact, because the effective length grows from $L_{min} - 2L_D$ to $2L_{min} - 2L_D$ when the drawn length doubles (more than double the effective length), and $V_{TH}$ shifts with $L$; so the reference curves are simulated for a few lengths, e.g. 60, 80 and 100 nm. Minimum length stays in the signal path wherever speed matters.

blocks.title: Sizing for a power budget and a swing
blocks.text: A resistively loaded CS stage at $V_{DD} = 1$ V may draw 0.6 mW and must stay saturated down to $V_{DS} = 0.2$ V. Simulations of the 5 µm/40 nm reference at $V_{GS} - V_{TH} = V_{DS} = 0.2$ V give $I_D = 100\,\mu$A, $g_m = 1.5$ mS and $r_O = 8$ kΩ. Size the device and find its $g_m$ and $r_O$.
solution: Current: $0.6\text{ mW}/1\text{ V} = 600\,\mu$A, so scale by 6: $W = 30\,\mu$m.

blocks.title: Given $g_m$ and $I_D$
blocks.text: A device needs $g_m = 6$ mS at $I_D = 0.5$ mA. Is it possible ($\xi = 1.5$, $V_T = 26$ mV)? If the reference curve passes through (150 µA, 1.8 mS), how wide must it be?
solution: Upper limit: $0.5\text{ mA}/(1.5 \times 26\text{ mV}) = 12.8$ mS > 6 mS, so it is possible.
Target $g_m/I_D = 12\text{ V}^{-1}$; the reference point also has $1.8/0.15 = 12\text{ V}^{-1}$, so it lies on the same line.

blocks.title: Overdrive from $g_m/I_D$
blocks.text: In strong inversion, what overdrive corresponds to $g_m/I_D = 10\text{ V}^{-1}$? How much current gives 1 mS at $g_m/I_D = 10$ and at 20?
solution: $I_D = g_m/(g_m/I_D)$: 100 µA at 10, 50 µA at 20 (the latter in moderate inversion, wider and slower).

blocks.title: Mobility degradation
blocks.text: A device has $\mu_0C_{ox}W/L = 10$ mA/V² and $\theta = 2\text{ V}^{-1}$. Find $g_m$ at an overdrive of 0.2 V, the square-law value, and the large-overdrive limit.
solution: Square law: $10\text{ m} \times 0.2 = 2$ mS. Limit: $\frac{1}{2} \times 10\text{ m}/2 = 2.5$ mS.
